svg.text: The baby in distress, and what to do with your hands first
Normal
Foetal heart 110 to 160 beats a minute
Listen for a full minute, during and just
after a contraction — not between them
Half-hourly in active first stage; every 5 minutes in second stage.
Worrying
Under 110, or over 160, sustained
A rate that does not recover after the
contraction has finished
Thick meconium with an abnormal rate
First response — before you call, and while you call
1. Turn her onto her LEFT side. The pregnant uterus compresses the vena cava when she lies on her back,
and less blood returning to her heart means less blood reaching the placenta.
2. Stop any oxytocin infusion that is running.
3. Give oxygen, and run intravenous fluid.
4. Examine: is the cord prolapsed? How far has the head descended? Then call for urgent help.
Position, then stop the oxytocin. Those two cost nothing and work in seconds.
Cord prolapse — the one where your hand stays where it is
Call for help and prepare for immediate caesarean section.
Push the presenting part off the cord with your gloved hand and keep it there, all the way to theatre.
Position her knee-chest, or head down on her side, to take the weight off the cord.
Do not try to push the cord back in. Handle it as little as possible; handling makes it spasm.
The cord is being squeezed between the head and the pelvis. Your hand is the only thing relieving it.
Suspect it whenever the membranes rupture and the heart rate drops, especially if the head was still high.
